Hey, Happy New Year! Here’s hoping that 2025 treats you with kindness, joy, and success!
There’s something about January that feels so refreshing, right? Whether we admit it or not, the new year comes with a ‘fresh start’ energy, prompting many of us to do things differently. What makes this first month inspirational is also influenced by the month that precedes it—December.
When you think of December, there’s this mental image of a snowy Christmas (even though it doesn’t snow in most parts of India), relaxed workdays, travel, and those hard-to-resist year-end sales. It’s a month when our willpower takes a break, and we allow ourselves to indulge a little more.
And many sellers take advantage of it - from Black Friday to Pink Friday sales, End of Season Sales to End of Reason Sales, shopping apps make us believe we’ll miss out on a great deal if we don’t ‘Buy Now.’
One thing that really helped me with online shopping is to create a wish list. It’s my way of mindful shopping. I add items that I like to the wish list instead of buying them immediately. After a day or two, I look back at the list and feel ‘meh’ about a lot of items. It turns out there’s even research to support this behaviour. It suggests that wishlisting can reduce impulse buying. Well, it indeed worked for me.
There seems to be another side to it. After adding items to a wish list, the emotional connection to saved items can grow, making the purchase feel even more tempting. What do you think and how do you control your impulse buying?
‘Mindful spending’ - while the most common financial resolution is to spend less, we suggest focusing on mindful spending - spending within our means and intentionally.
After all, some of the best things in life do come with a price tag - travelling to new places, pursuing hobbies or a new skill, or even treating yourself—these are the costs that feel like they’re worth it. Having said that, what’s the point in going beyond what we could afford? This is why ‘mindful’ is the word we lean on.
To save and invest more - is the next natural step after mindful spending. But many of us tend to delay investing, leaving our money idle in savings accounts. Why? It's much easier than to make the decision of where to invest, especially with so many options available.
Here’s a story on how a small ‘nudge’ can encourage us to invest more. This is from the book - Better Decisions for Health, Wealth, and Happiness, co-authored by Nobel Laureate Richard Thaler.
For a retirement plan, employees at a company were initially asked to fill out a form giving details like how much they’d like to save and how they wanted their money invested. Since filling out a form is an uncomfortable task for many, participation was low.
Then, they introduced automatic enrolment. Employees were automatically enrolled in the retirement plan with a default savings rate. If they wanted to make any changes, they could opt out and fill out the form. The result? Automatic enrolment helped participation soared from 20% to 90%. And what’s even more interesting is that once enrolled, most employees didn’t opt out. This is because of inertia bias—people prefer the status quo and didn’t want to take action to change it. Another reason is that many employees discovered they were saving more than they had expected.
For investors in India, the best nudge happened in the form of Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) from mutual funds. With SIP, a pre-decided amount is automatically deducted from your account every month. It removes the need to make a decision on where to invest. They are easy to set up,too, and gives you the freedom to stop anytime.
Nudging is often used in marketing and may not always be in the best interest of consumers. But SIP is an example of ‘nudge for good’ - a win-win for both investors and the financial system.
If my guess is right, I know what you must be thinking by now—while SIPs are an easy way to invest, the initial decisions of how much to save and where to invest are still ours to make.
I get it—these decisions depend on individual circumstances, and there’s no one-size-fits-all solution. At Varsity, we’re not big fans of thumb rules because they simply don’t work for everyone.
To conclude, spending less and investing more are the two most common financial goals—even for seasoned investors. If we could stay mindful of these and avoid easily preventable mistakes, like taking on too much debt or missing credit card payments, we’re already off to a strong start for the new year.
- Satya Sontanam

Whenever we’re excited about trying something new, there’s always that one person who says, ‘Oh, it’s hard’ or ‘It might not work.’
Just as we thought we started the new year with decent financial goals—cutting expenses and investing more—the markets seem to be doing their best to drain our motivation.
The markets have been mostly in the red zone for the year to date. In fact, from the highs of September 2024, the Nifty 50, mid-cap, and small-cap indices are down by 10% or over.
We are not used to this kind of market correction in the last few years, and it might start to make us feel uncomfortable.
Let’s take a step back and ask ourselves—what did we know about the markets, and what didn’t we?
What we knew: Markets are volatile, and ups and downs are a natural part of market cycles.
If we knew the probability of markets going down is as high as markets going up, why are we still stressed? Maybe it has something to do with what we didn’t know.
What we didn’t know: The extent to which the market can fall and how long it takes to recover.
This unpredictability creates stress, especially when our financial goals are linked to markets.
What we knew and what we didn’t know doesn’t matter when what’s happening is hurting us. Morgan Housel worded it better:
"Knowing the high odds of something happening loses its meaning when that thing happening hurts. Probability goes out of the window."
So, it’s natural to feel stressed. But what can we do about it? We have two options: stay invested or sell our investments and have peace of mind.
You would have heard a lot of ‘experts’ advising you to stay invested. Let’s dissect why.
I want to share what Howard Marks, an American investor and writer, said about risk.
He discusses two types of market risks and asks which is more risky— “1. buying at the high and seeing it decline; or 2. selling at the low and missing out on the recovery.”
Marks said, “Clearly, it's the latter.”
“You buy at a high, and you experience a decline. If you are able to hold throughout and not lose your nerve, then the next high is usually higher than the last high.
The fact that you experienced a downward fluctuation might have been a little uncomfortable for a while, but by the time the new high is achieved, you are back to your cost and more.
But if you sell at the bottom and miss out on the subsequent recovery, you have gotten off the investing track and may never get back on.
In my opinion, selling at the bottom is the cardinal risk of investing.”
This makes sense unless it is an utterly bad investment or at an exorbitant valuation.
So, the best thing we can do when markets are playing up is to accept their nature and simply do nothing. If you have some extra cash and can stay invested long-term, taking advantage of the low market levels to invest is also not a bad idea.
While market risk can’t be entirely avoided, it can be managed. A highly regarded word in investing is ‘asset allocation.’
This means diversifying your assets, holding debt assets like FDs for short-term needs, and equity for long-term goals. Following this could be of great help.
So yeah, while the markets may be testing our patience right now, don’t write them off just yet. In the long term, they might turn out to be a supporting friend, too.
- Satya Sontanam
